script.opening: "Hi doctor, calling about one of our residents, Edna, 86, she's got a bit of dementia normally but the last day or two she's gone really confused and agitated — up all night, picking at things, not herself at all. The staff are struggling. Could you prescribe something to settle her down, a sedative or one of those antipsychotics? We just need her calmer, really."

facts.text: You are Grace, senior carer/nurse on shift at Meadowbank care home. You know Edna well.
Mild dementia. Normally chatty, knows staff by name, walks with a frame, feeds herself, sleeps through the night, sometimes forgets what day it is.

Over the last 36 hours: much more confused, worse in the evening and at night, better for short spells in the morning. Picking at the air, says she can see "children in the corner". Shouting at staff. Not slept last night. Sleepy at times during the day.

facts.topic: Observations — only if asked to do them
facts.text: You go and check while on the phone: temperature 37.9°C, pulse 102, BP 118/70, breathing rate 20, oxygen saturation 95% on air. She is not drowsy enough to be hard to wake.
Drinking much less — "maybe half her usual". Fewer wet pads than usual and the urine smells strong. Bowels not opened for four days.
If asked to check the MAR chart: co-codamol 30/500 started last week by the out-of-hours doctor for knee pain, two tablets four times a day. Her other medicines: amlodipine and donepezil.
No falls, no cough, not short of breath, no vomiting. Allergies: none recorded. No DNACPR or ReSPECT form changes recently; family (son) visits weekly.
Two carers short on nights; one carer was scratched last night. You are worried about the other residents being disturbed.

Busy, stressed, a bit insistent. Ask for "something to calm her" at least twice. If the doctor explains that this is likely delirium caused by something physical and asks good questions, help willingly. If they refuse sedation with no explanation, get frustrated: "So what do I do tonight?" Respond well to a concrete plan (urine sample, fluids, stop the co-codamol or reduce it, treat constipation, a visit, what to do overnight).

ice.ideas: "Her dementia's got worse — she needs something to calm her down."
ice.concerns: Staff are stretched, a carer was scratched, other residents are being disturbed.
ice.expectations: "Can you prescribe a sedative or an antipsychotic?" You will follow a different plan if it is practical and clear.

cues: "She's not herself at all." — say in the opening.
"She's seeing children in the corner." — say if asked what she is doing.
"The out-of-hours doctor started her on something last week." — say only if asked about new medicines.

checkpoints.text: Recognises this as ACUTE DELIRIUM (acute, fluctuating change in cognition/alertness on a dementia background, with hallucinations and sleep-wake disturbance) — a sign of underlying physical illness — NOT a behaviour to sedate, and does not simply prescribe a sedative/antipsychotic on request

Systematically seeks the CAUSE(S): infection (UTI/chest — urine, obs, fever), constipation, dehydration/reduced intake, pain/urinary retention, and crucially the NEW MEDICATION (anticholinergic/sedative/opioid) — a "PINCH ME"-type screen — and plans assessment/examination, bloods and a medication review

Prioritises NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL management: treat the precipitant, plus reorientation, familiar staff/faces, hydration, sleep hygiene, glasses/hearing aids, pain relief, mobilisation and treating constipation — before any sedation

Recognises the HARMS of antipsychotics/sedatives in delirium/dementia (falls, stroke, increased mortality, worsening delirium) and reserves them as a LAST resort for severe distress/risk to self or others, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, with review

Has a clear plan and threshold for ESCALATION: in-person assessment (GP visit), and admission if she is systemically unwell / cause cannot be managed in the home / safety concerns — not leaving a potentially septic elderly patient sedated and unassessed
SUPPORTS the stretched, overwhelmed staff with empathy while NOT colluding with inappropriate chemical restraint — redirecting firmly but kindly to finding the cause and using non-drug measures
Frames the approach around the patient’s dignity and best interests (and the staff’s genuine difficulty), gaining their cooperation with the work-up

Safety-nets and acts: the cause work-up and review/visit plan, non-drug measures, red flags for urgent escalation/admission (deteriorating, septic, unsafe), documentation, and a follow-up — treating the delirium’s cause, not chemically restraining the patient

worked.txt: "Thank you for ringing — and I can hear the staff are really stretched. But before any sedative, the key thing is this: a sudden change like this over a day or two, on top of her usual dementia, isn’t just ‘her dementia getting worse’. It’s what we call delirium, and it’s almost always a sign her body is unwell with something we can find and treat. Sedating her would calm the ward but miss what’s actually wrong — and those drugs carry real risks for her, including falls and worse."

"So let’s find the cause together. You mentioned offensive urine and she’s a bit warm — that points to a possible infection. Is she constipated? How’s she drinking? And crucially — was any new medication started recently? … Last week, yes. All of those — infection, constipation, not drinking, a new drug — are classic triggers, and they’re treatable."

"While we sort the cause, the things that genuinely help her settle aren’t sedatives: keep her calm and reoriented, familiar staff where you can, her glasses and hearing aids on, plenty to drink, light in the day and quiet at night, deal with any pain or constipation. Those reduce the agitation safely."

"I’m going to come and assess her / arrange an assessment — examine her, check a urine sample and her obs, and review that new medication. If she’s clearly unwell with an infection that the home can’t manage, or she’s deteriorating, we may need to get her to hospital. I don’t want to leave an 86-year-old sedated when she might have a treatable infection."

"I’m not saying we’d NEVER use a calming medicine — if she became severely distressed or a danger to herself, we might, briefly and at a tiny dose, and reviewed. But it’s the last step, not the first, and only alongside treating the cause."

"I do appreciate how hard this is when you’re short-staffed — you’re doing the right thing by calling rather than just managing it. Let’s get the urine and obs done, I’ll assess her, and ring me back if she becomes more unwell, drowsy, or you’re worried about her safety. We treat what’s making her like this — we don’t just switch her off."

f.learning: Acute, fluctuating confusion and agitation over hours–days on a background of dementia — with hallucinations and sleep-wake disturbance — is DELIRIUM, a sign of underlying physical illness, NOT a behaviour to be sedated on request. The task is to find and treat the cause(s): a systematic screen (infection — UTI/chest; constipation; dehydration/reduced intake; pain/retention; and crucially a NEW MEDICATION, often anticholinergic/sedative/opioid — "PINCH ME"), with assessment/examination, urine, obs, bloods and a medication review. Non-pharmacological measures come FIRST (treat the precipitant, reorientation, familiar faces, hydration, sleep hygiene, glasses/hearing aids, pain relief, mobilise, treat constipation); antipsychotics/sedatives carry real harms in delirium/dementia (falls, stroke, increased mortality, worsening delirium) and are a last resort for severe distress/risk only, at the lowest dose with review. The examinable hidden agenda is a stretched, overwhelmed care home seeking chemical restraint to manage a staffing problem; support the staff with empathy while NOT colluding — redirect to the cause and non-drug measures, assess in person, and escalate/admit if she is septic or unsafe.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG103 (2010, updated 2023) — delirium · NICE NG97 (2018) — dementia · NICE NG253 (2025) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (December 2021)
knowledge.summary: An acute, fluctuating change over 24–48 hours in a woman with mild dementia — agitation, sleeplessness, picking at the air — is delirium until proven otherwise. The task is to find and treat the cause, not to sedate the symptom.

points.t: NICE CG103: be alert to recent changes or fluctuations in behaviour — cognition, perception (hallucinations), physical function (reduced intake, sleep disturbance) and social behaviour (agitation, withdrawal). A sudden change in someone with dementia is delirium until shown otherwise. The 4AT is a quick structured assessment.

NICE CG103: identify and manage the possible underlying causes. Here: possible infection (fever, offensive urine), constipation, reduced intake and dehydration, and a medicine started last week. Also consider pain, urinary retention, hypoxia and electrolyte disturbance. Review the new drug first.

UKHSA urinary tract infection diagnostic guidance: do not use urine dipsticks in people aged over 65 — asymptomatic bacteriuria is common. Base the decision on clinical features and send a urine sample for culture if infection is suspected.

NICE CG103: in a distressed person, first use verbal and non-verbal de-escalation. Reorientation, familiar staff, glasses and hearing aids, hydration, treating constipation and pain, daytime light and a quiet night reduce agitation without drug harms.

NICE CG103: if distressed or a risk to themselves or others and de-escalation fails, consider short-term haloperidol (usually for 1 week or less), starting at the lowest clinically appropriate dose and titrating cautiously — dose per BNF. Use antipsychotics with caution or not at all in Parkinson’s disease or dementia with Lewy bodies. MHRA Drug Safety Update (December 2021) highlights the risks of haloperidol in elderly patients with delirium.

A GP visit the same day, with observations (NEWS2) and examination. Sepsis risk judged per NICE NG253; admit if she is systemically unwell, the cause cannot be managed in the home, or she is unsafe. Do not leave a possibly septic older woman sedated and unassessed.

dg.d: Identifies caller and resident; open question; lets the nurse describe the change before responding to the sedation request.
Staffing pressure, falls worry, Edna’s usual baseline and who else should be informed.
Same-day visit; full observations; urine culture (no dipstick over 65); fluid and bowel charts; bloods at the visit; medication review.
Delirium versus progression of dementia; infection, constipation, dehydration, drug effect, retention, pain.
Sepsis risk via observations and NICE NG253; asked about Parkinson’s or Lewy body before any antipsychotic.
Acute delirium with several likely precipitants — explained to the nurse in plain terms.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Cause-first plan, non-drug measures, no sedative on request; short-term low-dose haloperidol only as a last resort per NICE CG103.
Reviews the new medicine; treats constipation and dehydration; falls precautions; next of kin informed.
Visit today; ring back with observations; 999 triggers named; summary agreed.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “not herself”, “picking at things”, the strong-smelling urine and the new medicine.
The home’s idea (her dementia is worse), concern (short-staffed, falls) and expectation (a sedative or antipsychotic).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Staff are stretched, a carer was scratched, other residents are being disturbed — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, this is Dr Clarke. Can I take your name and role, and the resident’s full name and date of birth? … Thank you. Tell me what’s been happening with Edna.
model.why: Identifies caller and patient, then an open question

model.text: She’s got a bit of dementia normally, but the last day or two she’s gone really confused and agitated — up all night, picking at things, not herself at all. The staff are struggling. Could you prescribe something to settle her, a sedative or one of the antipsychotics? We just need her calmer.
Thank you for calling — it sounds like a really hard couple of days for you and the team. I want to help. Can I ask some questions first, so we treat whatever is making her like this?
model.why: Acknowledges the staff’s pressure before redirecting

model.text: Yes, of course.
What is Edna usually like on a good day, and how quickly did this change come on? Does it come and go?
model.why: Baseline, acute onset and fluctuation — the core of delirium

model.text: Normally she’s just a bit forgetful with her dementia. This came on over a day or two. Some moments she’s better, then she’s off again.
Is she eating and drinking? How are her bowels and her urine?
She’s hardly drinking. Fewer wet pads, and it smells quite strong. And she hasn’t had her bowels open for a few days.
Have you taken her observations — temperature, pulse, blood pressure, breathing, oxygen?
model.why: Objective data for sepsis risk (NG253 / NEWS2)

model.text: Her temperature’s up a little. I can do a full set now.
Please do, and ring them through to me. Has anything changed with her medicines recently?
model.why: Asks directly about the new drug

model.text: She was started on something new last week. I’d need to check the MAR chart for the name.
That’s really important — please have the chart ready for me. Does she have Parkinson’s disease, or a diagnosis of Lewy body dementia?
Just mild dementia, as far as I know.
What’s your biggest worry at the moment, on the unit?
model.why: Explores the caller’s real concern behind the request

model.text: Honestly, we’re short-staffed. She’s been up and down all night, and I’m worried she’ll fall. We just need her settled.
That’s a completely fair worry, and a fall would be serious. Thank you for being honest about the staffing — let’s make a plan that keeps her safe and doesn’t leave you on your own with it.

What you’re describing — a sudden change over a day or two, coming and going, with her picking at the air — is delirium, not her dementia getting worse. Delirium almost always means her body is unwell with something, and here there are several clues: possible infection, constipation, not drinking, and a new medicine.
model.why: Names delirium and its likely precipitants

model.text: So you don’t want to give her anything?

Not as a first step. A sedative would quieten her but hide what’s wrong — and in someone her age with dementia those drugs can make confusion worse and increase the risk of falls, stroke and death. If we treat the cause, the agitation usually settles.
model.why: Explains antipsychotic harms and the cause-first approach

model.text: Okay. That makes sense, I suppose.

Here’s the plan. I’ll visit her today. Before I arrive: the full set of observations, a urine sample for the lab rather than a dipstick, a fluid chart, and encouraging drinks. Please have the MAR chart ready so we can review that new medicine.
model.why: Same-day assessment and a cause work-up

model.text: We can do that.

Meanwhile, the things that genuinely help: a familiar member of staff with her where possible, glasses and hearing aids in, calm reassurance, a low bed or other falls measures you use, light in the day and quiet at night.
model.why: Non-drug measures that also address falls risk

model.text: What if she gets really distressed before you arrive?

Ring me straight away. If she became severely distressed or a danger to herself despite all that, a small short-term dose of a calming medicine can be considered — but as a last resort, alongside treating the cause, and reviewed daily.
model.why: Sedation positioned as a reviewed last resort per NICE CG103

model.text: If her observations are worrying, she becomes very drowsy or hard to rouse, breathless, or stops drinking altogether, call 999 — don’t wait for me. Could you also let her next of kin know what’s happening, in line with her records?
model.why: Clear escalation triggers; involves family appropriately

model.text: Yes. I’ll do the obs now and ring you back.

Thank you — you did exactly the right thing ringing. Just so we’re agreed: obs now, urine to the lab, fluids and bowels, MAR chart ready, non-drug measures, I visit today, and 999 if she deteriorates.
Got it. Thanks, doctor.

social.t: Short staffing and night-time disruption drive requests for sedation. Acknowledge it and offer practical support rather than judgement.
Familiar faces help delirium. Next of kin should be informed of the change, in line with her records and any lasting power of attorney.

legal.t: Delirium may remove capacity for treatment decisions. Decisions are made in her best interests, consulting those close to her and any health and welfare attorney. Restraint — including chemical restraint — is lawful only if necessary to prevent harm and proportionate (section 6).
Using medicines to control behaviour for staff convenience can amount to improper treatment. CQC regulation 13 requires care homes to protect people from unnecessary or disproportionate restraint.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only with enough information about the patient’s condition. An antipsychotic for new confusion without assessment falls short.
A new medicine last week is a likely contributor. Review, record any adverse reaction, and feed back to the prescriber without blame.

community.t: Community frailty or care-home support teams, district nurses, and older people’s mental health services for persistent behavioural symptoms. Alzheimer’s Society resources on delirium for families and staff.

redFlags: Acute, fluctuating change over hours to days — delirium, not dementia progression
Fever, rising NEWS2, drowsiness, breathlessness — sepsis risk (NICE NG253), consider 999 or admission
Parkinson’s or Lewy body dementia — antipsychotics with caution or not at all
psychosocial: Staffing pressure and fear of falls on a busy night
Edna’s baseline and who knows her best
Next of kin and any lasting power of attorney
ice: Expectation: a sedative or antipsychotic to settle her

playbook.diagnosis: Clear and supportive: “A sudden change over a day or two, coming and going, is delirium — it means her body is unwell with something, and there are several clues we can act on.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Delirium is like the brain’s warning light coming on. Covering the warning light with a sedative doesn’t fix the engine — we need to find what’s wrong underneath.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re short-staffed and worried she’ll fall — that’s a real concern. Let’s make a plan that keeps her safe and treats what’s making her like this.”
management.psychosocial: Give the home specific, doable tasks and a clear route to call back; recognise the staff’s effort.
sharedPlan: Same-day GP visit: examination, observations, bloods; urine culture (no dipstick over 65)
Review the new medicine; treat constipation; fluid chart and encourage drinks
Non-drug measures first; short-term low-dose haloperidol only as a last resort per NICE CG103, dose per BNF
safetyNet: Worrying observations, drowsiness, breathlessness, stopping drinking → 999
Ring back with observations; ring immediately if severely distressed or unsafe

pitfalls.intro: A third-party telephone call with a clear request: the station tests whether you treat the caller’s problem or the patient’s. It is failed on prescribing to order, and on handling the nurse badly.

items.fail: Prescribing a sedative or antipsychotic over the phone because the home asked.
items.why: NICE CG103 requires the cause to be identified and managed; antipsychotics increase falls, stroke and mortality in older people with dementia.
items.fix: “Before any medicine, we need to find out why she’s changed — this sounds like delirium.”

items.fail: Accepting “her dementia is worse” without asking about onset and fluctuation.
items.why: Acute, fluctuating change is the hallmark of delirium — the diagnosis is made in the history.
items.fix: “What is she like on a good day, and how fast did this come on?”

items.fail: Asking for a urine dip and treating a positive result.
items.why: UKHSA guidance advises against dipsticks over 65; a positive dip may hide the real cause, such as the new drug or constipation.
items.fix: Urine culture, full observations, bowels, fluids and a medication review — then examine.

items.fail: Lecturing the nurse about chemical restraint.
items.why: “Does not work in partnership.” The home carries out the plan; a defensive caller won’t.
items.fix: Name the pressure first — “I can hear you’re short-staffed” — then offer practical steps.

items.fail: Advice only, with no assessment arranged.
items.why: A possibly septic 86-year-old needs examining; remote advice alone is unsafe.
items.fix: “I’m going to visit today — please have her observations and MAR chart ready.”

items.fail: No escalation triggers or call-back plan.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback, and delirium can deteriorate quickly.
items.fix: Name 999 triggers, ask for the observations to be rung through, and summarise the plan.

timeMap.d: Who is calling, about whom. Let the nurse describe the change and make the request.
Baseline, onset, fluctuation; intake, bowels, urine; observations; the new medicine; Parkinson’s or Lewy body.
Staffing and falls worries. Validate them — then redirect.
Delirium, not worse dementia. Why not sedation. Visit today, urine culture, fluids, bowels, medication review, non-drug measures.
999 triggers, ring back with observations, next of kin, summary.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes a sedative or antipsychotic over the phone on request; accepts “her dementia is worse”; no search for infection, constipation or the new drug; no visit arranged; or lectures the nurse and loses her cooperation.
wordPics.pass: Recognises delirium; asks about infection, intake, bowels and the new medicine; declines sedation as a first step; arranges assessment; gives escalation advice.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: supports the stretched nurse genuinely; checks for Parkinson’s or Lewy body; avoids dipstick reliance; gives specific non-drug measures that also address falls; positions haloperidol correctly as short-term last resort; summarises a plan the home can actually carry out.

avoid.dont: “I’ll send over some haloperidol to calm her down.”
avoid.instead: “A sudden change like this is delirium — let’s find what’s making her unwell first.”
avoid.why: Sedating on request misses the cause and adds serious harms.

avoid.dont: “We don’t use chemical restraint — you’ll have to manage.”
avoid.instead: “I can hear you’re short-staffed. Here’s what will genuinely help, and I’m coming to see her.”
avoid.why: Criticising the caller loses the partnership you need.

avoid.dont: “Dip her urine and I’ll start antibiotics if it’s positive.”
avoid.instead: “Please send a urine sample to the lab rather than dipping it, and I’ll examine her.”
avoid.why: Dipsticks mislead over 65; delirium needs a broader cause search.

SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call from a care-home nurse requesting “something to settle her”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG103 (2010, updated 2023) — delirium · NICE NG97 (2018) — dementia · NICE NG253 (2025) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (December 2021)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: An acute, fluctuating change over 24–48 hours in a woman with mild dementia — agitation, sleeplessness, picking at the air — is delirium until proven otherwise. The task is to find and treat the cause, not to sedate the symptom.

points.t: NICE CG103: be alert to recent changes or fluctuations in behaviour — cognition, perception (hallucinations), physical function (reduced intake, sleep disturbance) and social behaviour (agitation, withdrawal). A sudden change in someone with dementia is delirium until shown otherwise. The 4AT is a quick structured assessment.

NICE CG103: identify and manage the possible underlying causes. Here: possible infection (fever, offensive urine), constipation, reduced intake and dehydration, and a medicine started last week. Also consider pain, urinary retention, hypoxia and electrolyte disturbance. Review the new drug first.

UKHSA urinary tract infection diagnostic guidance: do not use urine dipsticks in people aged over 65 — asymptomatic bacteriuria is common. Base the decision on clinical features and send a urine sample for culture if infection is suspected.

NICE CG103: in a distressed person, first use verbal and non-verbal de-escalation. Reorientation, familiar staff, glasses and hearing aids, hydration, treating constipation and pain, daytime light and a quiet night reduce agitation without drug harms.

NICE CG103: if distressed or a risk to themselves or others and de-escalation fails, consider short-term haloperidol (usually for 1 week or less), starting at the lowest clinically appropriate dose and titrating cautiously — dose per BNF. Use antipsychotics with caution or not at all in Parkinson’s disease or dementia with Lewy bodies. MHRA Drug Safety Update (December 2021) highlights the risks of haloperidol in elderly patients with delirium.

A GP visit the same day, with observations (NEWS2) and examination. Sepsis risk judged per NICE NG253; admit if she is systemically unwell, the cause cannot be managed in the home, or she is unsafe. Do not leave a possibly septic older woman sedated and unassessed.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Identifies caller and resident; open question; lets the nurse describe the change before responding to the sedation request.
Staffing pressure, falls worry, Edna’s usual baseline and who else should be informed.
Picked up “not herself”, “picking at things”, the strong-smelling urine and the new medicine.
The home’s idea (her dementia is worse), concern (short-staffed, falls) and expectation (a sedative or antipsychotic).
Same-day visit; full observations; urine culture (no dipstick over 65); fluid and bowel charts; bloods at the visit; medication review.
Delirium versus progression of dementia; infection, constipation, dehydration, drug effect, retention, pain.
Sepsis risk via observations and NICE NG253; asked about Parkinson’s or Lewy body before any antipsychotic.
Acute delirium with several likely precipitants — explained to the nurse in plain terms.
Cause-first plan, non-drug measures, no sedative on request; short-term low-dose haloperidol only as a last resort per NICE CG103.
Reviews the new medicine; treats constipation and dehydration; falls precautions; next of kin informed.
Visit today; ring back with observations; 999 triggers named; summary agreed.

social.t: Short staffing and night-time disruption drive requests for sedation. Acknowledge it and offer practical support rather than judgement.
Familiar faces help delirium. Next of kin should be informed of the change, in line with her records and any lasting power of attorney.

legal.t: Delirium may remove capacity for treatment decisions. Decisions are made in her best interests, consulting those close to her and any health and welfare attorney. Restraint — including chemical restraint — is lawful only if necessary to prevent harm and proportionate (section 6).
Using medicines to control behaviour for staff convenience can amount to improper treatment. CQC regulation 13 requires care homes to protect people from unnecessary or disproportionate restraint.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only with enough information about the patient’s condition. An antipsychotic for new confusion without assessment falls short.
A new medicine last week is a likely contributor. Review, record any adverse reaction, and feed back to the prescriber without blame.

community.t: Community frailty or care-home support teams, district nurses, and older people’s mental health services for persistent behavioural symptoms. Alzheimer’s Society resources on delirium for families and staff.

redFlags: Acute, fluctuating change over hours to days — delirium, not dementia progression
Fever, rising NEWS2, drowsiness, breathlessness — sepsis risk (NICE NG253), consider 999 or admission
Parkinson’s or Lewy body dementia — antipsychotics with caution or not at all
psychosocial: Staffing pressure and fear of falls on a busy night
Edna’s baseline and who knows her best
Next of kin and any lasting power of attorney
ice: Expectation: a sedative or antipsychotic to settle her

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Clear and supportive: “A sudden change over a day or two, coming and going, is delirium — it means her body is unwell with something, and there are several clues we can act on.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Delirium is like the brain’s warning light coming on. Covering the warning light with a sedative doesn’t fix the engine — we need to find what’s wrong underneath.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re short-staffed and worried she’ll fall — that’s a real concern. Let’s make a plan that keeps her safe and treats what’s making her like this.”
management.psychosocial: Give the home specific, doable tasks and a clear route to call back; recognise the staff’s effort.
sharedPlan: Same-day GP visit: examination, observations, bloods; urine culture (no dipstick over 65)
Review the new medicine; treat constipation; fluid chart and encourage drinks
Non-drug measures first; short-term low-dose haloperidol only as a last resort per NICE CG103, dose per BNF
safetyNet: Worrying observations, drowsiness, breathlessness, stopping drinking → 999
Ring back with observations; ring immediately if severely distressed or unsafe

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: A third-party telephone call with a clear request: the station tests whether you treat the caller’s problem or the patient’s. It is failed on prescribing to order, and on handling the nurse badly.

items.fail: Prescribing a sedative or antipsychotic over the phone because the home asked.
items.why: NICE CG103 requires the cause to be identified and managed; antipsychotics increase falls, stroke and mortality in older people with dementia.
items.fix: “Before any medicine, we need to find out why she’s changed — this sounds like delirium.”

items.fail: Accepting “her dementia is worse” without asking about onset and fluctuation.
items.why: Acute, fluctuating change is the hallmark of delirium — the diagnosis is made in the history.
items.fix: “What is she like on a good day, and how fast did this come on?”

items.fail: Asking for a urine dip and treating a positive result.
items.why: UKHSA guidance advises against dipsticks over 65; a positive dip may hide the real cause, such as the new drug or constipation.
items.fix: Urine culture, full observations, bowels, fluids and a medication review — then examine.

items.fail: Lecturing the nurse about chemical restraint.
items.why: “Does not work in partnership.” The home carries out the plan; a defensive caller won’t.
items.fix: Name the pressure first — “I can hear you’re short-staffed” — then offer practical steps.

items.fail: Advice only, with no assessment arranged.
items.why: A possibly septic 86-year-old needs examining; remote advice alone is unsafe.
items.fix: “I’m going to visit today — please have her observations and MAR chart ready.”

items.fail: No escalation triggers or call-back plan.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback, and delirium can deteriorate quickly.
items.fix: Name 999 triggers, ask for the observations to be rung through, and summarise the plan.
